I'm new to editing and would like to know if we have any linuxers in /v/editing that can provide any guidance!

I'll say all that I can, but you aren't going to like it. Nothing past adobe CS3 suite works well in wine. AE and Premier CS3 work, but have some serious issues. Photoshop and Illustrator CS3 work well and don't suffer as many drawbacks as AE and Premier.

PHOTOSHOP: Image editing is hard on linux, the best all-around image editor in linux is GIMP. GIMP is the only all-in-one Photoshop alternative on linux. There are plugins and UI mods to make it very similar to Photoshop. There is also a plugin that emulates Photoshop compatibility and allows you to STRAIGHT UP use Photoshop plugins. Inkscape is another program amazing for vector graphic work.

AFTER EFFECTS: Blender is a 3d + composting program that can replace AE, although it does take some time and a fair bit of tweaking to get to work in a similar fashion. If you don't mind using non-free (free as in $$$) software, you can try NUKE STUDIO. Nuke Studio comes with its own composting program, NukeX and it's own editor Nuke Hiero. It is a node-based editing program, not a layer based one so getting used to it can take a bit. (But nodes are so much more efficient in workflow in my experience.)

PREMIER: If you don't mind spending $$$$ (and a lot of it) You can get DaVinci Resolve. DaVinci is an amazing replacement for premier, but it only runs on centOS, which is your choice to get or not. For free alternatives, Openshot is good if you are used to classical NLE layered editors, but it does not include the same sort of functionality as Premier. Lightworks is another NLE program that has a large learning curve, but can prove quite powerful and compatible.

If you'd prefer your entire workflow be kept in a single suite, Nuke is your best bet. Otherwise, feel free to check and see what you like best!

I've only really dabbled a bit, but I've run across a few different editors of various kinds. Some free, some not.

Image editors

GIMP (free): I've worked with some web designers that have had experience in Photoshop and GIMP. Almost unanimously they all say that Photoshop can do so much more, but what I heard between the lines was "Photoshop has a ton of macros that do things that GIMP doesn't have." From what I could understand it's possible for GIMP to be just as powerful but it would take some serious work on the part of the developers or community, or both, to create some plugins that would rival what Photoshop can do. This is just my opinion.

Bloom Image Editor ($50 USD): This seems to have some really cool methods of handling how changes are applied, so that it keeps a history of all changes and easy to undo something based on layer, not the order it was done in.

Inkscape (free): This one handles vector graphics really well. I haven't really met anyone who has used this and the Adobe alternative enough to give a good comparison.

Video Editors

Kdenlive (free): A multi-track video editor, seems to be a really popular.

CinelerraCV (free): I've played with this one a little some time ago and it seemed really powerful but with a really steep learning curve. It may have gotten better since then (they seem to have merged some stuff). They tout being able to handle BluRay quality video files.

Blender (free): This one I would say could nearly rival After Effects, but with the same opinionated caveats as Gimp/Photoshop. On YouTube there is a number of channels where people will show you how to do some really cool effects (e.g. lightsabers, plasma balls, replace what's on a billboard, etc). There is a very good chance we are alone; the Fermi paradox doesn't take into consideration statistical mechanics and entropy (I guess U Chicago spent all of their money on nuclear reactors in squash courts).

Life == a (temporary) violation of the Second Law of Thermodynamics which is (virtually impossible) to violate for macroscopic ensembles.

Because these violations are absurdly unlikely it follows that life is absurdly unlikely. I feel this is a better explanation than the Drake equation, and it fairs better to occham's razor as well.

While entropy acts on all things, people included, it acts upon the individuals not on a species in total. Each of us must die of old age (entropy again), but our species lives on as long as we can reproduce our kind before we die.

but even for an individual I would think a temporary increase in entropy is unlikely. Always fun to ponder the Fermi paradox. First of all, I think the article drastically overstates the odds of life developing. It admits (as I do) that this is all ultimately speculative, but as far as we know the chances of life developing are ridiculously small, even on a planet capable of hosting that life (which, as @BBQue points out, is probably rare in the first place). So far at least, we've discovered no firm evidence of life occurring on any planet other than our own, and given the lack of evidence the most plausible conclusion is that it simply hasn't happened anywhere else (or at least not in our galaxy where we can see said evidence).

As for the various "type 2" hypotheses, I find them all unpersuasive for the reason the article has already given: the rule of exceptions. Could there be ridiculously advanced entities that we can't even observe, let alone understand? Of course. Could there be entities that are deliberately not contacting us? Certainly. But even in those scenarios, what are the odds that not a single species breaks from the general rule? One would expect that in a universe with hugely advanced species, there would also be less advanced species that we can observe. The only hypothesis that tackles this problem is the "superpredator species" hypothesis, but that's a bit spectacular to believe without further evidence.

Completely speculative conclusion: we're either the only intelligent species to have made it this far or among the first such that others haven't yet developed enough or existed long enough to contact us.
